Title: Ballyhoo
MainText:
Coin-operated pin bagatelle machines were made at a breakneck pace. At the height of the Great Depression these games were produced cheaply and quickly, offering new distractions, and ideas had to come just as fast. It was easiest to simply copy them.

Raymond Moloney wanted to make his own pin bagatelle machine, having issues sourcing and distributing Gottlieb's best-selling *Baffle Ball* (Gottlieb, Nov. 1931). Rather than develop it from scratch, he looked to the popular magazine Ballyhoo—the *MAD* magazine of the 1930s—and simply used their colors and style. He even kept the title the same and called his company Bally, though this machine is labelled with Bally's parent company, Lion Manufacturing.

Title: Carom
MainText:
After Bally's success with *Ballyhoo*, their business exploded. Between *Ballyhoo* and *Carom*, they made more than 120 different models. As you can see, in just five years they became larger, more complex, and more automated. The window on the backbox shows the score, an exciting innovation called a **totalizer**.

This is an example of a payout machine, where you might get more money out than you put in. This feature arguably made it a gambling machine, causing concern about how pinball was corrupting the youth, encouraging vice, and supporting criminals. However you see it, it was big business: 45 of those 120 models made by Bally gave payouts.

Title: Trade Winds
MainText:
When electricity was added to pin bagatelle, it served two functions: making the score easier to read and making everything about the machines more attention-grabbing. Compared to traditional pin bagatelle, *Trade Winds* is a leap forward on both accounts.

Rather than look around the playfield doing mental math, this machine keeps track of everything on its backbox. At the same time, it features a cohesive theme, sounds, and lights that are designed to tempt players from across the room. Some later pinball machines shout into the room when sitting idle—this is the 1945 equivalent.

Title: Baseball
MainText:
Chicago Coin, like other major manufacturers, stopped producing machines in 1942 to support the US's effort in World War II. Production resumed in 1945, making machines similar to those in the early 1940s. The central figure on the backglass likely references the then-popular All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, which started 1943, and whose story was told in *A League of Their Own*.

One month after this machine left the factory, Gottileb release the first machine with flippers, *Humpty Dumpty.* This machine's flippers were added later, likely by an operator updating his older machines to match the new craze.

Title: Derby Day
Ownership: The Flip Collection, accessioned from the collection of Sam Harvey
MainText:
*Derby Day* promises buckets of points but, like horse racing, success dangles by a thread. The flippers are far apart, the player is at the mercy of a pop bumper beneath them, and a "gobble hole" in the middle of the board will quickly end a ball, though it rewards some points in the process as compensation. Still, compared to earlier machines like *Trade Winds*, *Derby Day* focuses on keeping the game going, if in a chancy, nonlinear way.

As you play, you can hear the points racking up. Every function of electromechanical machines like *Derby Day* is connected to parts that whir and move. This machine has been fitted with a Plexiglas rear so you can see all the complex machinery at work in the backbox.

Title: Teacher's Pet
Ownership: The Flip Collection, accessioned from the collection of Sam Harvey
MainText:
As players gained more control over pinball machines, games grew longer. The modern flipper placement of *Teacher's Pet* lets players keep the ball in play, and the addition of free games granted by high scores—invented by Bill Belah in 1934—made the idea of indefinitely long play even more tangible. *Teacher's Pet* features a free ball gate on its right-hand outlane that saves the ball when activated.

Adding free plays was also a way of showing that pinball was not for gambling. Some manufacturers embraced this, while others doubled down on payouts—until pinball was banned in Chicago. Although this machine was made here, it could not be played in the city.

Title: Hokus Pokus
MainText:
While pin bagatelle machines operate in one direction—down—and flippers keep the ball in play, playfields had to change for a player to do more than just keep the ball alive. Compared to *Teacher's Pet*, the lanes in *Hokus Pokus* are easier to target from each flipper. On the left-hand side, this allows the ball to travel all the way to the start of the playfield, where bumpers and targets can rack up the points.

These points are also part of how pinball has developed. As time goes on, machines have offered higher and higher scores. The last score wheel in *Hokus Pokus* is actually fake, automatically multiplying any score by ten.

Title: Star Trip
Address: 140 Lively Blvd, Elk Grove Village IL
MainText:
The rise of transistors and computers made possible pinball's move from electromechanical to solid state logic in the mid 1970s. At the same time, the re-legalization of pinball created a bigger market. That meant opportunities for new companies to try their hand at pinball. One of those companies was Game Plan (1978-1985).

Cocktail table video games were already popular in 1974 and 1975. As their name suggests, they allowed bar owners to get in on the video game craze without losing space for patrons. A number of companies made cocktail pinball machines. But pinball wasn't as compelling in the smaller form, and manufacturers, Game Plan included, soon turned to full-sized machines.

The space theme surely references *Star Wars,* released in 1977. Note the ship suspiciously similar to an X-Wing fighter.

Title: Star Trek
MainText:
Bally's *Star Trek* is the first machine based on the *Star Trek* franchise, followed by Data East's 1991 *Star Trek*, Williams' 1993 *Star Trek: The Next Generation*, and Stern's 2013 *Star Trek*. It was made in connection with Paramount's December 1979 movie *Star Trek: The Motion Picture*. The most common backglass, seen here, shows the uniforms from that movie. Prominent placement of popular characters was a selling point; the machine's flyer says, "Immediate recognition of characters draws players directly to Star Trek."

A good example of early electronic sound in pinball, the game moves beyond the previous mechanical 3-bar chime set to add a variety of meaningful sounds and short tunes.

Title: The Incredible Hulk
MainText:
In the late 1970s, pinball jumped to the digital age: older electromechanical machines were replaced by new "solid state" games, typified by their use of transistors. Going digital opened new possibilities for pinball. In *The Incredible Hulk*, sounds are not limited to physical objects inside the machine and include a broad range of effects. Lights, too, got flashier. In some machines, bonuses could also now be carried from one ball to the next, even with multiple rotating players.

Players' ability to pick up where they left off also enriched these games' narratives. *The Incredible Hulk* arranges its bonuses in a ladder, giving a linear progression to its gameplay. Later machines would turn this progression into full-blown quests and missions.

Title: Blackout
MainText:
As Chicago has been the gravitational center of pinball design and manufacturing for decades, so too have Chicago-based artists been integral to pinball art. For Blackout, Williams reached out to the painter Ed Paschke (1939–2004), who was an important member of the Chicago Imagists, a group redefining contemporary art in their own surreal style. Many Imagists were influenced by pinball—as demonstrated by a 2017 exhibition at the Elmhurst Art Museum—and Paschke himself owned a *Gorgar* machine (Williams, December 1979).

Unfortunately for Paschke, his avant-garde style was not what Williams wanted. After producing his concept painting for this machine, also titled *Blackout* (1980), the company thought it was too "far out." Its amorphous, masked astronauts, its multicolored cosmic rays, and its pock-marked green planet were too strange. The company tapped Constantino Mitchell—himself a student of Ray Yoshida, another Chicago Imagist—to redesign Paschke's painting in a more conventional style. But, according to Mitchell, "I want Ed Paschke to get credit for [the] *Blackout* backglass design. He did the original art concept. Ed Paschke was my teacher and mentor at the Art Institute of Chicago. His usage of color influenced me for the rest of my life."

Paschke went on to curate an exhibition of pinball art in 1982 at the Chicago Cultural Center with Mitchell's collaboration.

Ed Paschke, *Blackout*, 1980. Oil on canvas; 30 × 36 in. (76.2 × 91.4 cm). Private collection. Photo courtesy The Ed Paschke Foundation.

Title: Hyperball
MainText:
Williams’s tagline shows the scope of their ambition: “First pin. Then video. Now HYPERBALL: the next revolution in games.” With pinball under threat from video games like Space Invaders (1978), Asteroids (1979), and Pac Man (1980), Williams attempted a synthesis of steel ball mechanics and the video shooter format.

Williams hoped that Hyperball would sell 50,000 units, but it flopped, selling only 5,000. Players found it loud and operators complained about wear and tear given the 55 balls being fired up to 250 times per minute in active, high-velocity play. Today, many pinball fans insist that Hyperball is not pinball at all.

To play it, think of it like a video game. The lightning bolts are trying to destroy your base. Shoot them before they get you!

Title: Eight Ball Deluxe Limited Edition
MainText:
A successor to the popular *Eight Ball* from 1977, *Eight Ball Deluxe* added more rules, more complicated shots, and speech synthesis. It was another hit, winning the Amusement Machine Operators Association award for Game of the Year in 1983.

The first version of this game, *Eight Ball Deluxe*, launched in April 1981, quickly sold 8,250 machines. This version, *Eight Ball Deluxe Limited Edition*, sold 2,388 units. It plays the same but has an unusual backbox, reusing the leftovers from Bally's answer to *Hyperball*, *Rapid Fire* (1982). Demand continued, so Bally Midway released a third version of it, also called *Eight Ball Deluxe*, in 1984.

Title: The Getaway: High Speed II
MainText:
Created by prolific pinball designer Steve Ritchie, this is the sequel to his 1986 hit *High Speed*. Making use of the then-new dot matrix display (DMD), *The Getaway* does away with the permanent score displays prominent since the 1940s. Instead, a grid of LEDs is used to show not just scores but information and basic animations.

Machines of the DMD era mark a new horizon for innovations in pinball. Alongside this new display, music and extensive sampled sound enriches the game, while the playfield expands into three dimensions with ramps and wireform habitrails. Earlier generations of pinball machines tend to reuse stock components with visual changes but, from the DMD era forward, bespoke toys and features become common for each machine.

Title: The Addams Family
MainText:
*The Addams Family*, the best-selling flipper pinball machine of all time, is widely loved. It was based on the 1991 comedy/horror movie *The Addams Family*, which was based on the 1964 television series and New Yorker cartoons from Charles Addams that ran from 1933 to 1964.

It uses both samples from the movie and custom audio recorded by actor Raul Julia. It was also the first pinball machine to make use of "artificial intelligence": a simulated neural network drives the "Thing Flips" feature, which automatically shoots the ball from the small upper left flipper to The Swamp on the right. And keep an eye out for the disembodied hand, Thing, which might take your ball.

Title: Godzilla (Premium)
MainText:
One of the best selling games in recent decades, Stern's *Godzilla* is a great example of a modern pinball machine. Instead of the earlier dot-matrix display, it uses full-motion video on an LCD screen. It has rich sound, a very colorful playfield, and makes extensive use of single-color and RGB LEDs to create a compelling light show.

Also common is that *Godzilla* is based on licensed material. This provides an instant audience for the machine. Here, Stern made extensive use of the Shōwa era Godzilla films (1954–75) to provide both a structure for the game and video clips to keep players engaged and bystanders entertained.

Title: Revenge From Mars
Info2: John Youssi, Greg Freres, et al
MainText:
Just a few years after *Addams Family* sold a record number of machines, the pinball industry was in serious decline. They no longer just had arcade games to compete with. The mid-1990s saw the introduction of home consoles: the Sega Saturn, Sony Playstation, and Nintendo 64 sold more than 140 million units between them.

In an attempt to turn things around, Williams launched Pinball 2000, a system that overlaid a video game monitor on top of the traditional pinball playfield via Pepper's ghost, a Victorian-era projection trick. But richer animation, sound, and interactivity were not enough. Only two Pinball 2000 models were produced, with *Star Wars Episode I* coming out in June 1999. Williams closed their pinball division permanently on October 25, 1999.

Title: Comet
MainText:
*Comet* is modelled after Riverview Park, a prominent amusement park that operated from 1904 to 1967 in Chicago's Roscoe Village. This machine expands pinball's narrative formats, turning the game into a leisurely day where point targets become activities: go-karting, motorcycle stunts, and riding the Comet. For *Comet*'s artist, Python Anghelo, this scene manifests what pinball should be: "a miniature amusement park [where] poor kids could go to fulfill their fantasies, changing into the ball ... for twenty-five cents."

However, Anghelo's optimism obscures how *Comet* echoes Riverview Park's history as a site of overt racism throughout the 1950s and 60s. *Comet* centrally features the park's dunk tank, which the NAACP succesfully lobbied to shutter due to its racist references, and the backglass displays a "pickaninny," a derogatory caricature of a Black child.

Title: Aztec (EM)
MainText:
One of the most popular electromechanical pinball machines of the 1970s, Aztec is a good example of the peak of that technology. It allowed for four players, had clear goals, and players could accumulate large bonuses.

However, the technology was already becoming obsolete. Williams made 10 copies of Aztec with solid state technology (including digital logic and LED displays) as an experiment. Less than 2 years later, Williams made their last electromechanical machine.

YouTube watchers may be familiar with "Old pinball machines are amazingly complex" from Technology Connections, a detailed look at electromechanical technology, which used Aztec as the main example.

Title: Aztec (SS)
MainText:
Compare this machine with its neghbor, *Aztec (EM)*. The main visible difference is that most of the numbers have been replaced with 7-segment digital displays. But the real differences are inside. The backbox, previously full of metal, is now nearly empty. The main body, which used to have many pounds of relays and switches, now has some modestly sized circuit boards.

This prototype gave the Williams engineers practical experience with computerizing a pinball machine, allowing them to switch entirely to digital logic for *Hot Tip* in November 1977.

Title: High Score
MainText:
This pin bagatelle machine reflects a period when many manufacturers rapidly entered the pinball market, often producing simplified games closely modeled on popular existing designs rather than introducing major innovations of their own. The Dean Novelty Company, based in Tulsa and run by T.J. Dean, was sued over *High Score* due to their patent-infringing use of a ball-reloading mechanism.

Although made for a commercial context, this machine was previously owned by a dentist from Tulsa. It was installed in a private vacation cabin in Noel, Missouri, for his personal amusement. After the cabin was sold, the machine sat untouched for decades before being relocated to Chicago in 2026.

Title: Tempest
MainText:
*Tempest* is a seminal video game that expands the shooting genre, taking the format of *Space Invaders* (1978) and wrapping it around a three-dimensional landscape. *Tempest* was also one of the first video games to feature progressive level design, where each level takes a different form and character, rather than simply increasing the game’s difficulty within the same layout.

The popularity of *Tempest* and games like it furthered competition with pinball machines in the early 80s. Pinball was not yet three-dimensional, as it would become in the DMD era, and so pinball designers turned to other changes to maintain machines’ appeal in arcades. One of the most radical is *Hyperball* (December 1981), located nearby, which responds to games like *Tempest* to reinvent what pinball might be.

Title: Space Cadet 3D
MainText:
Space Cadet 3D is a virtual pinball table, created as part of the 1995 commercial game *Full Tilt Pinball*. It was included with many versions of Microsoft Windows starting with Microsoft Plus. Along with *Solitaire* and *Minesweeper*, also free with Windows, it is instantly recognizeable to millions. For many, this was their first pinball experience.

That has given it a lasting fan base that keeps it alive today. After it was removed from windows, instructions for re-adding it were common. It was recently reversed engineered and ported to many platforms, including MacOS, Android, and even the Wii. It was also sampled in Lil Uzi Vert's *You Better Move* in 2020.

Here it appears on period-authentic hardware running Windows 98.

Title: Add-A-Ball
MainText:
In November 1960, Gottlieb released *Flipper*, the first add-a-ball game. Before *Flipper*, games were a fixed number of balls, with no extra balls. The only player reward was free games. But in some areas, those were considered a "thing of value" that was banned by gambling laws. Add-a-ball machines did not give replays, just extra balls.

Williams copied the feature, releasing this game less than a year later. Gottlieb quickly notified Williams that they could not use the name, so only a few of these were made before the name was changed to *Skill-Ball*.

Title: Kicker
Info1: Al Schlappa, Jerry Koci, John Gore
MainText:
Starting in 1964, the US experienced the British Invasion, a wave of popularity for many things British, kicked off by The Beatles, but including *Mary Poppins*, James Bond, *Lawrence of Arabia*, *The Saint*, and the miniskirt. An interest in soccer and the 1966 World Cup, held in England, followed. Chicago Coin's *Kicker* took avantage of all that, also making a version called *AAB* for export to Italy.

Note the backbox animation, an electromechanical version of something that become commonplace starting with dot matrix displays in the 1990s.

Title: Stock Car
MainText:
This is the add-a-ball version of Gottlieb's *Road Race*, rewarding pinball players with extended play rather than extra games, allowing these machines to be sold in areas where giving free games violated anti-gambling laws. That was a smaller market; *Road Race* sold 1425 units vs 350 for this game.

Note the wedgehead backbox design common in this era. Previously, single-player machines had narrower backboxes like *Kicker* does. But players often complained that they were packed too tightly in arcades to play. The trapeziodal design helped the machine take up space without having to make a larger backglass, as well as adding visual flair.

Title: Monopoly
MainText:
With the closure of Gottlieb in 1996 and Williams in 1999, pinball nearly died. But Gary Stern, son of the former Williams president Sam Stern, bought Sega's pinball division and kept the game alive, making one title in 1999, two in 2000, and 4 in 2001.

Monopoly, based on the Parker Brothers board game originally launched in 1935, is a good example of what became Stern's formula for success: colorful, lively games based on widely recognizeable licensed themes. Interestingly, this is not the first pinball game based on Monopoly; in 1936 Chicago coin created "Monopolee", a one-ball payout game with a theme involving property and mortages.

Title: Pin Bagatelle
MainText:
The ancestor of pinball is pin bagatelle. This game is a miniature version of a cue sport whose own origins go back to 1777 and the French court of Louis XVI. Its first appearance in English sources came later in 1819, and the game became popular throughout the US in the nineteenth century.

Pin bagatelle balls were originally launched with a miniature cue stick. This game boasts an important addition from 1871: the spring plunger, patented by Montague Redgrave, which became a staple of pin bagatelle and pinball alike.

To play this game, players score points by landing balls in targets. If a ball lands in "R," all non-scoring balls at the bottom can be replayed. But if a ball lands in "X," gameplay ends immediately.
